article.articleHeadline: Democratic Republic of the Congo - Ebola response: Disinformation kills, care saves lives
article.articleSummary: EBOLA in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues to show that disinformation can kill while care saves lives. In Rwampara and Ituri, demystification sessions, community dialogues and training of 100 traditional healers, 20 social media influencers and 150 hotline operators improved access to reliable information. article.articleHeadline: Origin Path with You | Plague reservoir hosts have not yet gone extinct — How does Hong Kong guard against imported plague cases?
article.articleSummary: Pneumonic plague caused by Yersinia pestis poses imported risk to Hong Kong after a laboratory incident in Irkutsk, Russia, where a female technician broke a live sample and died of severe pneumonia. Pneumonic plague spreads by droplets and can kill within hours if untreated; incubation about 24 hours and mortality approaches 100%. Globally, droplet transmission fuels rapid clusters; historic context includes 1910 Wu Lien-teh work in Northeast China that demonstrated human-to-human spread. Natural reservoirs persist in Eurasian grasslands and forests, so sporadic foci remain even with modern controls. The World Health Organization 2021 plague-control report notes persistent wild rodent reservoirs and occasional cases in remote areas. Hong Kong’s Centre for Health Protection has ramped up surveillance and containment readiness to guard against imported cases; authorities emphasize vigilance and public hygiene, not panic, leveraging lessons from past outbreaks and available isolation facilities.

article.articleHeadline: In rural Shandong, free influenza vaccinations for the elderly and the young exceed 2.36 million.
article.articleSummary: Shandong Province launched free one-dose trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine for rural residents: seniors aged 65+ and primary/secondary school students, starting Sept 29. The rollout combines fixed sites with mobile outreach, including extended hours and weekend sessions. A WeChat mini-program enables online identity verification and one-click appointment by matching resident ID and age to eligibility; for those unable to use smartphones, relatives, village doctors, or care facility staff can book on their behalf, enabling 'no-contact' screening and reduced queues. Vaccination sites maintain health screening, 30-minute post-vaccination observation, and stocked emergency meds. The effort is coordinated by city and provincial health, education, and civil affairs departments, to ensure vaccine supply and nearby access, with messaging to vaccinate before the influenza season peak.

article.articleHeadline: Hong Kong Department of Health email account suspected of being impersonated; many people received information about the risk of HIV infection.
article.articleSummary: On October 24, 2026, the Hong Kong Department of Health announced that an email account used by its HIV testing service appears to have been misused to impersonate the department and send false information claiming recipients are at risk of HIV infection. The department is conducting a serious investigation and, so far, has found no evidence of data loss or leakage. The messages—whether by email or SMS—were not issued by the Health Department, and officials will not notify individuals in this manner. Citizens who receive suspicious emails or texts should remain vigilant, avoid clicking any links, and refrain from sharing personal information. If personal data has already been provided or scam suspicions arise, individuals should contact the police immediately. The incident highlights cybersecurity risks in public health communications involving sensitive conditions such as HIV.

article.articleHeadline: Full coverage! Qingdao rabies exposure management outpatient clinics' tetanus service coverage reaches 100%.

article.articleHeadline: Alarming scientific discovery: seafood may transmit a vision-threatening infection.
article.articleSummary: As of 26 October 2026, researchers from China, Australia, and Singapore link marine virus CMNV to an emergent human eye disease labeled POH-VAU. In a study of 70 patients, the disease’s anterior segment causes recurrent inflammation and chronically elevated intraocular pressure, risking optic nerve damage and vision loss. Laboratory analyses detected CMNV in ocular tissues and immune markers indicating prior infection, supporting a virus-eye disease connection. The study highlights a marine-origin spillover from aquatic animals to humans, with the most common exposure routes being direct handling of fish and shellfish during cleaning/preparation and consumption of undercooked or raw seafood; together these factors accounted for about 71.4% of cases. Repeated exposure to contaminated aquatic environments correlated with higher risk. Preventive measures include gloves, thorough handwashing, avoiding raw seafood, and prompt ophthalmologic evaluation for redness, pain, blurred vision, or recurrent inflammation.

article.articleHeadline: His own car has become a "bird toilet"; a Guangdong man inexplicably diagnosed with pneumonia; doctors say there have already been several such cases; a gentle reminder: bird droppings should not be wiped away casually.
article.articleSummary: Guangdong pneumonia case linked to pulmonary cryptococcosis from inhaling dust of dried bird droppings on a car, reported by Shenzhen Songgang People’s Hospital; several similar cases exist in the respiratory department. Earlier incidents occurred in 2023 (Taizhou, Zhejiang) and 2025 (Chongqing), where a 60-year-old woman presented cough and chest imaging abnormalities; serum cryptococcal antigen was positive, confirming infection. Cryptococcus yeast thrives in damp, nutrient-rich bird droppings (notably pigeons); inhaled dust can cause lung infection, sometimes resembling tuberculosis or tumors, and can involve the CNS. Transmission is not person-to-person. Four risk factors: pathogen presence in droppings, dry state increasing dust, exposure dose/mode, and immune status. Prevention/cleaning: avoid dry wiping; wear mask and gloves; dampen droppings for 3–5 minutes, wipe gently, rinse, and seal/dispose of used materials. Clean promptly, ideally the same day or within 1–2 days.

article.articleHeadline: PGK1 kinase activity disables a host chaperone to restrict multiple viruses
article.articleSummary: PGK1, a glycolytic enzyme, acts as a non-canonical protein kinase to restrict replication of multiple viruses by targeting the host chaperone HSP90AA1. In vitro and mouse studies from the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences show PGK1 binds and phosphorylates HSP90AA1, reducing its chaperone activity and increasing K27-linked ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. As HSP90AA1 declines, viral proteins dependent on the chaperone become unstable and are degraded, inhibiting replication of influenza A virus, Sendai virus, vesicular stomatitis virus, and herpes simplex virus 1. This host-directed antiviral mechanism operates independently of PGK1’s glycolytic function and may reflect a broader defense strategy. Influenza A nucleoprotein can compete with HSP90AA1 for PGK1, suggesting a viral immune evasion tactic. Findings published in Science China Life Sciences, with mouse data; researchers view PGK1-HSP90AA1 as a candidate broad-spectrum antiviral axis, not yet clinical.

article.articleHeadline: Norovirus infections in China linked to CNY 20.23 billion annual medical
article.articleSummary: Norovirus infections in China were detected in 18.80% of acute gastroenteritis patients tested across four provinces from 2018–2024 (23,527 patients), with national annual direct medical costs estimated at CNY 20.23 billion. Inpatients had higher positivity (26.15%) than outpatients (13.78%), and children under five showed the highest age-specific rate (30.49%). Among norovirus-positive patients, 18.97% had at least one potential concurrent complication, most commonly dehydration (11.28%), followed by convulsions (5.52%). The clinical pattern is age-dependent: children under five experience more severe manifestations, while adults 65+ incur higher per-case hospital costs; median inpatient cost 4,580 CNY (IQR 3,129–6,402) versus 230 CNY for outpatients (IQR 128–354). National estimates stem from combining multicenter data with census and epidemiological data; results are limited by sample representativeness of four provinces. The study supports age-targeted public health strategies and regionally tailored resource allocation.

article.articleHeadline: Research report: Clinical epidemiological characteristics of Omicron
article.articleSummary: Shanghai Pudong Hospital retrospectively analyzed 4,173 patients hospitalized with SARS-CoV-2 Omicron BA.2 infection (April–June 2022). Among them, 934 (22.38%) had hypertension. Most hypertensive patients had asymptomatic or mild disease; 32 deaths occurred in this subgroup (3.4%), all unvaccinated, with 71.9% having more than one underlying condition. Multivariable analyses linked vaccination to lower odds of moderate/severe disease (OR 0.280, 95% CI 0.143–0.548) and higher lymphocyte counts to protection (OR 0.608). Pulmonary infection markedly increased risk of moderate/severe illness (OR 5.422); elevated hs-CRP also associated with higher odds (OR 1.006). For mortality, chronic kidney failure carried the largest risk (OR 5.701); theophylline use (OR 5.063) and elevated D-dimer (OR 1.092) also associated with death, though CIs were wide. Protective factors included higher lymphocyte proportion (OR 0.920) and higher albumin (OR 0.865). Limitations: single-center, retrospective, limited period; causality not established. Most hypertensive BA.2 infections in hospitalized patients were not severe.

article.articleHeadline: Influenza subtypes show distinct meteorological drivers in Shanxi
article.articleSummary: Influenza subtypes in Shanxi Province, China, show distinct meteorological drivers based on laboratory-confirmed surveillance from 2009–2024 (excluding COVID-19 NPIs). Among 29,246 cases, A(H1N1)pdm09 accounted for 28.7%, A(H3N2) 39.6%, and influenza B 31.7%. Using a two-stage random-forest approach and subsequent univariate and multivariate models, researchers found absolute humidity to be the most robust protective factor across subtypes, while each subtype responded to different weather patterns. A(H1N1)pdm09 was sensitive to low temperature and humidity and high wind speed, with high temperature reversing wind-risk. A(H3N2) was associated with higher solar radiation and higher temperature, with a synergistic protective effect. Influenza B linked to a humidity–pressure system, where high humidity offset risks linked to high pressure. The study notes caution: data from one province, lab-confirmed cases only, unable to fully separate meteorology from other transmission influences; implications for subtype-specific early-warning models.

article.articleHeadline: Interpretable machine learning model stratifies latent tuberculosis risk
article.articleSummary: In Henan Province, China, a multicenter case-control study published open-access in BMC Public Health on 22 October 2026 enrolled 782 participants (401 latent TB infection and 381 newly diagnosed, treatment-naive pulmonary TB). Researchers built an interpretable machine learning model using only questionnaire-based epidemiological predictors to distinguish active pulmonary TB from latent TB infection and to stratify latent infection into three risk tiers for targeted follow-up. XGBoost achieved best performance (AUC 0.818; F1 0.764; Brier 0.176). A three-tier risk framework used probability cutoffs >0.763 (high) and <0.328 (low), with TB prevalence rising from 20.0% in the low-risk tier to 84.29% in the high-risk tier. SHAP analysis identified male sex, low BMI, older age, recent weight loss, and low annual household income as key drivers. A free web calculator translates the model for use in resource-limited settings, but external validation and prospective evaluation are required; data derive from a single province.

article.articleHeadline: Receptor EGFR helps swine diarrhea virus enter cells, study finds
article.articleSummary: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV), a coronavirus causing severe diarrhea, vomiting, dehydration and high mortality in suckling piglets, relies on host EGFR to enter cells. Researchers from Henan Agricultural University and the Henan Academy of Agricultural Sciences in Zhengzhou, China identified epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) as a co-factor promoting PEDV entry. Using Vero cells, they combined EGFR knockout with imaging to compare viral behavior. PEDV spike protein associates with EGFR. EGFR knockout impaired viral internalization, while attachment remained intact, indicating a role in internalization. PEDV particles colocalized with EGFR in early endosomes, late endosomes and lysosomes; loss of EGFR reduced colocalization with late endosomes, suggesting a role in post-internalization trafficking. The study concludes EGFR supports infection by promoting internalization and endo-/lysosomal trafficking—a dual role at entry stages, with only partial impairment upon knockout. Interaction with interferon signaling requires further study.

article.articleHeadline: Respiratory failure due to Influenza A.
article.articleSummary: An 88-year-old woman in Hanoi, Mrs. Mạo, developed influenza A with rapid respiratory failure; she initially lacked fever. At Tam Anh General Hospital Hanoi, she tested positive for influenza A. Chest X-ray showed bronchial thickening and bilateral infiltrates; labs indicated inflammation, myocardial stress, and bacterial coinfection. She has bronchial asthma, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and prior multi-territory strokes, complicating care. Influenza A can trigger asthma exacerbations and worsen heart conditions, increasing risk of pulmonary edema and respiratory failure. She received antiviral therapy, antibiotics, bronchodilators, expectorants, arrhythmia treatment, and non-invasive ventilation, and after more than a week was discharged. Emphasis on vaccination: annual influenza vaccine (A/H1N1, A/H3N2, B) for those 6 months+, with yearly boosters; vaccination reduces hospitalization and death by up to 90%, and lowers myocardial infarction and stroke risk by 15–45%. Co-circulating pathogens (RSV, pneumococcus, meningococcus) may coinfect; practice hygiene and seek early care for elderly with symptoms.

article.articleHeadline: Be vigilant about the risk of dehydration in children infected with Norovirus.
article.articleSummary: Norovirus is a common cause of acute gastroenteritis in children and adults, with recent cases reported at Nghệ An Obstetric and Pediatric Hospital in Vietnam. In Nghệ An, children presented with fever, vomiting, abdominal pain, and acute diarrhea, linked to Norovirus exposure. Transmission is fecal-oral via contaminated food, water, surfaces, or contact with an infected person; onset typically 12-48 hours after exposure, enabling rapid clusters in households, daycare centers, and schools. Rotavirus vaccine does not protect against Norovirus. Important dehydration signs include dry lips, sunken eyes, reduced tears, scant urination, and infrequent diaper changes. Home care prioritizes hydration with oral rehydration solution (ORS) in small, frequent sips, continuing breastfeeding or formula, and soft, easily digestible foods. Avoid antibiotics or antidiarrheals unless advised. Seek hospital care for persistent vomiting, inability to drink, high fever, severe abdominal pain, or signs of dehydration.

article.articleHeadline: Rising respiratory illnesses, warning of RSV risk in young children.
article.articleSummary: In Ho Chi Minh City, rising respiratory illnesses during the end of the year (October–December) are driven by weather changes, with RSV singled out as a leading cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in newborns and children under 12 months. At Children’s Hospital No. 1, about 300 children are currently treated in the respiratory department, with 60–80 new admissions daily; regional numbers have risen modestly versus last year but no abnormal trend yet. RSV often starts with fever, runny nose, and cough but can rapidly progress to wheezing, rapid breathing, chest retractions, poor feeding, or lethargy; severe cases may require respiratory support. Globally, RSV causes about 66,300 deaths annually in infants under 1 year. In Vietnam, RSV-related hospitalizations total tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands each year, some needing ICU care. Preventive measures emphasize hygiene, avoiding unnecessary antibiotics, maternal vaccination during pregnancy to pass antibodies to newborns, and direct monoclonal antibody prophylaxis for children.

article.articleHeadline: Lao Cai strengthens prevention and control of African swine fever.
article.articleSummary: October 2026 outbreaks of African swine fever in Lao Cai Province, Vietnam affected 67 households across 19 hamlets in 5 communes, with 462 pigs culled (over 23.5 tons). In ten months, the province recorded outbreaks in 392 households, 115 hamlets, across 34 communes, with 2,677 pigs culled (over 116.3 tons). Authorities maintain coordinated control measures including surveillance, zoning, stamping-out, vaccination, and environmental disinfection of farming areas. As of October 8, 22 of 34 communes had 21 consecutive days without new animal infections. Looking to year-end, the sector calls for stronger disease monitoring and guidance on biosecure farming to limit spread, protect livestock, and stabilize production. Coordination between agriculture and environment departments is emphasized. Public communication and farmer education programs are also highlighted.

article.articleHeadline: Bakery oven causes 352 people to suffer food poisoning, forcing more than 1 billion dong in compensation.
article.articleSummary: Salmonella-spurred food poisoning outbreak linked to Hong Ngoc 37 Bakery in Đạo Thạnh Ward, Đồng Tháp Province, sickened 352 people after meals on July 15–16. Laboratory confirmation from Ho Chi Minh City Pasteur Institute found Salmonella sp in 25 of 36 patient samples. The owner must cover all treatment costs, totaling over 1 billion VND; fines include 4 million VND for inadequate sanitation and 90 million VND for poisoning affecting five or more people. Hong Ngoc is a Mekong Delta bakery chain with over 100 branches; this marks the third mass poisoning incident, following 149 cases in August 2024 and 86 cases by April 2026.

article.articleHeadline: Vietnam's Dak Lak records 4 Whitmore's disease cases, including one death
article.articleSummary: Whitmore's disease (melioidosis) caused four cases in Vietnam’s Dak Lak Province in 2026, including one death. Two patients are from Ea Sup Commune, with one each in Buon Ho Ward and Tuy Hoa Ward. The deceased, N.V.R., 57, from Ea Sup, began symptoms Aug 7, was moved to Cho Ray Hospital (Ho Chi Minh City) on Sep 22, and died Oct 14 after returning home. The current case, L. B. H., 69, of Tuy Hoa Ward, is at Phu Yen General Hospital after presenting with high fever and back pain on Aug 17; admitted Sep 1, transferred to Cho Ray on Sep 20. A pus sample on Oct 9 tested positive for Burkholderia pseudomallei. He returned to Phu Yen General Hospital on Oct 13; condition gradually stabilizing. Source under investigation; potential exposure to contaminated soil or water; freshwater fishing reported; no vaccine available; disease does not spread person-to-person.

article.articleHeadline: Who infected with influenza A should be treated with antiviral drugs early?
article.articleSummary: Influenza A should be treated with antivirals early, especially in high-risk groups. Vietnam's National Hospital for Tropical Diseases advises prompt assessment and discourages self-medication. Most influenza A infections are mild and resolve in a week, but can progress to pneumonia and hospitalization in healthy individuals. High-risk groups include young children (especially under 2), the elderly (65+), pregnant women, and people with chronic diseases such as heart or lung disease, COPD, kidney or liver disease, diabetes, and neurological disorders; immunocompromised patients, cancer patients, organ transplant recipients. Obesity (BMI ≥ 40), aspirin use in those under 19, and residents of long-term care facilities also warrant vigilance. Oseltamivir should be prescribed and started within 48 hours of symptoms; adults typically receive 75 mg twice daily for five days, with weight-based dosing for children. Vaccination remains essential; seek emergency care for severe signs like shortness of breath, chest pain, confusion, dehydration, or fever in infants.

article.articleHeadline: Locals forced to live amid heaps of garbage, fear of an outbreak: in Munjka city it has taken hold, but facilities are zero and daily cleaning is not done, garbage piles up.
article.articleSummary: Munjka village, now within Rajkot city limits after expansion, suffers persistent filth with Street No. 7 lacking regular cleaning and no proper waste disposal. Public dumps grow into large garbage piles, emitting an unacceptable odor, as residents and nearby areas discard waste in open spaces. The ensuing mosquito nuisance raises fears of dengue and malaria outbreaks, posing health risks to children and the elderly. Despite multiple representations, local authorities have not acted, and residents demand immediate daily cleaning in Street No. 7. This situation underscores potential infectious disease risk (dengue, malaria) tied to poor sanitation and stagnant waste, with no reported case counts in the article but clear outbreak fears and urgent public health concerns.

article.articleHeadline: "Rabies suspected": A stray dog bit 16 people, including a child, in just a few hours.
article.articleSummary: Rabies suspected after a stray dog in Balumath, Latehar district, Jharkhand, India, attacked 16 people over several hours on Friday afternoon into the evening. Victims, aged 8 to 35, sustained a range of injuries, with three cases among the severely hurt: a woman with multiple leg wounds, a young man with his lower lip torn, and a child bitten on the nose, causing shock from bleeding. All were brought to a local medical center where rabies and tetanus vaccines were administered; health workers reported sufficient vaccine stocks and noted a full vaccination course will be required for all victims. Eyewitnesses said the same aggressive dog was seen near roadside cafes. The incident highlighted a gap: Latehar district lacks a dedicated stray-dog capture service. Officials plan measures to curb movement of dangerous animals and strengthen control at congregant areas.

article.articleHeadline: Chennai residents warned of dengue and rat fever, advised to drink boiled water
article.articleSummary: Chennai northeast monsoon advisory: Greater Chennai Corporation commissioner GS Sameeran warned of increased dengue and leptospirosis (rat fever) and diarrhoeal illnesses due to waterlogging and poor sanitation. Citizens should drink boiled, cooled water from safe sources, store in clean covered containers, and avoid floodwater-contaminated supplies; report contamination to GCC or Metro Water. Wash hands with soap before food preparation or meals; eat freshly cooked food; wash fruits and vegetables with clean water. For diarrhoea, use ORS and seek medical care if blood in stools, persistent vomiting, reduced urine, or dehydration; avoid self-medication. To curb mosquito-borne diseases, prevent water stagnation in discarded tyres, coconut shells, and flower pots; clean water storage weekly and keep covered; use repellents and wear long sleeves. For leptospirosis, avoid walking through floodwater without protective footwear and keep wounds covered. Contact UPHCs or government hospitals or GCC helpline 1913.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue outbreak wreaks havoc in neighboring Bangladesh, 2,249 new cases and seven deaths in 24 hours, adopt these precautions.
article.articleSummary: Bangladesh reports a dengue surge with 2,249 new cases and seven deaths in the last 24 hours, per the Directorate General of Health Services. This brings total dengue cases in 2026 to 123,948 and deaths to 384, with 117,400 recoveries. New fatalities occurred in Dhaka North (2), Mymensingh (2), and in Dhaka South, Khulna, and Rajshahi (1 each). Experts attribute rising deaths to a severe circulating strain, patients' comorbidities, and delays in hospital care, urging stronger coordination among primary, secondary, and tertiary health services to provide timely ICU/ventilator support. India may face dengue risk in November due to sustained warm temperatures that favor Aedes mosquitoes. Preventive measures include draining standing water from pots and coolers, wearing long sleeves, using mosquito repellents, securing entry points, staying hydrated, and seeking prompt medical care for fever after CBC testing; avoid NSAIDs before doctor's advice.

article.articleHeadline: New dengue scare in the state! Where did the laxity occur? A meeting at Health Bhavan today to probe.
article.articleSummary: West Bengal faces a dengue fever surge during Pujo. In the first 24 days of October, 2026, the state reported 5,751 new dengue infections. The total dengue cases in the year reach 12,889, with 15 deaths and 290 patients under treatment as of October 24. A high-level review at Health Bhavan was convened to probe gaps in dengue control, with participation from hospital authorities, secretaries, district magistrates, and municipal commissioners. The six most affected districts are Murshidabad, Kolkata, North 24 Parganas, Howrah, South 24 Parganas, and Malda. Experts cited weather changes and standing water as drivers of mosquito breeding; doctors urged vigilance. Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari acknowledged some progress but said he is not satisfied; he noted this year's figures and deaths are lower than last year. The outcome of the meeting will determine new measures.

article.articleHeadline: Alwar: Strict action on the reuse of medical equipment in hospitals; DGHS issues guidelines, calls for monitoring in Alwar | DGHS Guidelines Reuse Disposable Medical Devices Hospitals Alwar Infection Risk
article.articleSummary: DGHS guidelines ban reuse of single-use medical devices and disposable surgical supplies in all hospitals in Alwar, mandating strict compliance and regular infection-control monitoring. Reuse of one-time devices poses serious infection risks, including transmission of Hepatitis B and C, HIV, and bacterial infections, and can lead to reduced device efficacy and treatment complications, with reports of patients being charged full price for reused equipment. While reuse of older equipment is not automatically prohibited if standards and safety are maintained, the prohibited practice emphasizes that single-use items must not be reused. The DGHS letter to state health departments calls for immediate hospital inspections and the formation of rapid investigation teams to audit all hospitals and nursing homes in Alwar, ensuring infection-prevention measures. Violations may trigger action under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act (1940) and Medical Devices Rules (2017).

article.articleHeadline: Maharajganj News: Hepatitis B patients increasing in the district; 13 tested positive.
article.articleSummary: In Maharajganj district, Hepatitis B cases are rising. District hospital pathology reported 13 confirmed Hepatitis B positives in October among 723 individuals tested that month. Public health action includes enforcing timely vaccination, with government facilities providing the vaccine free of charge. Hepatitis B is a liver-targeting viral infection with two forms: acute (less than six months) and chronic (more than six months), the latter raising risks of liver cirrhosis and liver cancer. Symptoms include extreme fatigue, dark urine, abdominal pain, nausea, and jaundice. Transmission occurs via blood and body fluids, unsafe sex, reused needles, from mother to child at birth, and sharing razors. Officials urge vaccination of children on schedule and require infected individuals to receive regular medication and medical follow-up to control transmission.

article.articleHeadline: Electrician dies of leptospirosis near Kanyakumari.
article.articleSummary: One 31-year-old man, Subin, from Alandankarai near Rajakkamangalam in Kanyakumari district, died of leptospirosis after working as a field worker with Chennai’s electricity department. He developed fever, was treated at a private Chennai hospital where leptospirosis was diagnosed, and was brought back to his home region. He was admitted to a government medical college hospital in Acharippallam, but succumbed despite treatment. Police from Rajakkamangalam are investigating. Leptospirosis is caused by Leptospira bacteria and is commonly spread via the urine of infected animals (rats, dogs, cattle, and other mammals). Transmission occurs when people walk through standing water or mud contaminated by urine, especially during heavy rains in areas with poor drainage. Symptoms include severe fever, chills, headache, red eyes, muscle and abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea; red eyes are a key sign, and the disease can invade liver, kidneys, lungs, heart, pancreas, and brain.

article.articleHeadline: Scourge of the sex trade in Arwal: 43 new HIV cases identified, including 19 women.
article.articleSummary: HIV outbreak in Arwal district, Bihar, India, with 43 new infections identified by November 2026, on top of 390 patients already in treatment. Among the new cases, eight are pregnant women and 11 are non-pregnant women; a husband-wife pair in Vansi block tested HIV-positive but are not receiving treatment. Transmission is reported beyond the red-light area into hotels and marriage halls, with two raids conducted in these venues and two in the red-light zone; more than 20 people were brought to the police station, with adults released after warnings, and a festival hall raid two days earlier detained 10 individuals. Health officials are running targeted camps in high-incidence areas and increasing awareness and testing; government labs maintain records, while data from private labs remain incomplete. Authorities emphasize regular monitoring and law-enforcement actions to curb illicit activities as part of the containment effort.

article.articleHeadline: Tamil Nadu government appoints 33 senior entomologists amid gaps in disease surveillance
article.articleSummary: Tamil Nadu appoints 33 senior entomologists to strengthen district-level surveillance and control of vector-borne diseases—dengue, malaria, and chikungunya—amid vacancies in the public health workforce. Health Minister KG Arunraj distributed appointment orders to TNPSC-selected candidates at the Directorate of Medical and Rural Health Services campus in Chennai’s Teynampet. With entomologist posts vacant in more than 40 of 45 Health Unit Districts ahead of the northeast monsoon, the specialists will oversee vector surveillance, mosquito control, disease prevention, zoonotic infections monitoring, and coordination of national health programmes at the district level. Arunraj emphasized early intervention, transmission-pattern identification, and scientific surveillance, noting direct recruitment to senior entomologist posts has not occurred for nearly 30 years; of 69 state posts, only 17 were occupied, and 13 more will be recruited. Entomologists will guide vector-control by evidence beyond fogging; appointees urged to prioritise prevention and outbreak detection, with officials including Health Secretary Darez Ahamed in attendance.

article.articleHeadline: Hand Foot & Mouth Disease Symptoms: Has your child started going to school after the Puja holidays? If you see these signs on the hands and feet, beware... this disease can be highly contagious.
article.articleSummary: Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD), caused by Coxsackie virus, is a highly contagious viral illness in children. The article explains rapid spread from child to child, presenting with fever and vesicular rashes on hands (including palms and elbows), armpits, back, waist, knees, and feet, plus similar mouth lesions; symptoms can resemble chickenpox and make eating painful, but most cases resolve within about a week. Management emphasizes paracetamol for fever and pain, adequate fluids, and antihistamine lotion for skin discomfort; intravenous fluids or other supportive care may be required if oral intake is poor. Due to easy transmission, rest, isolation from others, and clinician guidance are advised. In India, HFMD shows seasonality from spring to autumn, with over 1 million cases annually, especially among children in play schools and day-care. After Puja holidays, caution as children return to school. Published 26 October 2026.

article.articleHeadline: Early Pyrethroid Resistance Detected in Dengue Mosquitoes from Southern
article.articleSummary: Aedes aegypti from Nagapattinam district, Tamil Nadu, southern India, shows early pyrethroid resistance with a heterozygous V1016G kdr mutation detected in field populations and reduced susceptibility to pyrethroids in WHO-guided bioassays. Homozygous GG mutants were not observed at this point, indicating an early stage of resistance under ongoing insecticide pressure. The study sequenced the vgsc gene via allele-specific PCR to identify the V1016G mutation and reported baseline data on the genetic mechanism of resistance in this dengue vector. Authors emphasize the need for regular monitoring of kdr mutations to detect resistance early and to guide insecticide-use policies. They advocate integrating molecular surveillance with conventional control measures to delay spread and improve long-term vector management. As a single-district snapshot, the heterozygous genotype distribution suggests progression toward broader resistance and underscores the need for alternative control strategies and responsible insecticide use.

article.articleHeadline: Nagaland private practitioners urged to follow updated TB treatment guidelines
article.articleSummary: As of 2026-10-26, Nagaland private healthcare practitioners in Kohima have been urged by the National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP) to adhere to government-prescribed TB prevention, diagnosis, and treatment guidelines. A sensitisation programme in Kohima highlighted aligning private-sector practice with national protocols to aid TB elimination, since many patients seek care from private clinics. Chief Medical Officer T Yetovi Tuccu warned that inconsistent treatment approaches threaten patient and public health. The initiative also stressed counseling for economically disadvantaged patients on completing the full TB therapy, noting that financial barriers and access issues can lead to treatment discontinuation, relapse, or the emergence of drug-resistant TB. Practitioners were urged to explain the importance of completing the course and refer patients needing assistance to government facilities for ongoing care.

Pur (Little Andaman), Hut Bay, and GSSS Bengali (Teressa Island), plus door-to-door campaigns in Diglipur, R.K. Gram and Subashgram. Sanitization was conducted at R.K. article.articleHeadline: Ticks in Kashmir Valley Carry Babesia bovis and Theileria Sequences, Survey
article.articleSummary: Across Kashmir Valley, India, a cross-sectional survey of 4,965 domestic ruminants found 1,800 tick-infested animals (36.27%). Haemaphysalis ticks dominated (84%). Molecular screening detected Babesia DNA in 19/1,800 ticks (1.06%) and Theileria DNA in 10/1,800 ticks (0.56%). Babesia-positive ticks came from cattle (3/720, 0.42%), sheep (14/720, 1.94%), and goats (2/360, 0.56%); Theileria occurred in cattle (5/720, 0.69%) and goats (5/360, 1.39%), with no positives in sheep. Babesia positivity was higher in female ticks (13/648, 2.01%) than males (3/792, 0.38%; P=0.004). Infestation peaked in summer. Phylogenetic analysis linked Kashmir Babesia with Babesia bovis and Theileria with Theileria cf. luwenshuni. The study provides baseline piroplasm surveillance data; limitations include detection of DNA and low positivity; recommends higher-resolution typing. Published online 26 Oct 2026 in Acta Parasitologica (vol. 71, art. 245).

In Goa, a recent campaign sterilised around 900 dogs with no rabies detected; another round is expected in about a month.

article.articleHeadline: Two Novel Silviavirus Phages Show Lytic Activity Against MRSA
article.articleSummary: Two novel Silviavirus bacteriophages, CARØ0038 and CARØ0046, show lytic activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and were isolated from sewage in Davangere, Karnataka, India. Genomes span 120,939 bp (CARØ0038) and 136,667 bp (CARØ0046) with 29.5% and 29.1% GC, encoding 227 and 225 predicted genes. Transmission electron microscopy indicates icosahedral heads with short tails (Caudoviricetes). Phylogenomic analyses place both in the genus Silviavirus, with species-level assignment unresolved. In vitro, latent periods are 15–20 minutes; burst sizes of 49 and 47 PFU per cell; an MOI of 0.1 yields the highest titres. Infectivity is retained up to 37°C but declines at 45–50°C and is undetectable after 60°C; optimal pH around 7 with activity from pH 6–8. The phages lyse all 28 tested MRSA isolates and also methicillin-susceptible S. aureus, but do not lyse S. epidermidis or S. saprophyticus under tested conditions. No antimicrobial resistance or virulence genes were detected. These data support further exploration as phage-based antimicrobials, noting taxonomic ambiguity and formulation considerations.

article.articleHeadline: Rains raise alert for diseases in dairy cows; losses could reach 98% of gross margin.
article.articleSummary: Rains in Brazil's dairy sector raise disease risk in cows, with humidity and mud boosting mastitis, hoof infections, leptospirosis and parasitic challenges. In Uberlândia, MG, CNA/Campo Futuro data (Cepea/ESALQ-USP) project annual mastitis losses of 8,000–14,400 reais, equal to 55–98% of gross margin for a typical dairy farm. Subclinical mastitis may reduce milk by 0.18–0.88 liters per affected teat per day, often undetected without somatic cell counts. Digital dermatitis can cut production by about 0.7 kg per cow per day; leptospirosis risks rise from contaminated water/soil, with reproductive issues and human health risks. Moisture also favors parasites and insects. Zoetis urges preventive management, clean resting areas, drainage, proper teat hygiene, surveillance (SCC), and veterinary oversight, plus vaccination and biosafety during the rainy season.

article.articleHeadline: Columbia scientists reveal how the malaria parasite invades human cells.
article.articleSummary: Malaria kills about 600,000 people annually, mostly African children under five, per the WHO. Columbia University researchers in New York have captured in action the mobile junction, the ring-like gateway the parasite uses to invade red blood cells. Using cryo-electron microscopy, they froze samples to preserve proteins and recorded the exact moment of entry: the junction opens a brief pore in the red blood cell membrane and then seals it as molecular clamps assemble and the cell surface is remodeled. The mobile junction is the entry route for all human-infecting Plasmodium species, making it an attractive drug target. Blocking it could stop blood-stage replication and guide therapies for related parasites causing cyclosporiasis and toxoplasmosis. In Brazil’s Amazon, malaria remains high (100k+ cases annually, mainly Plasmodium vivax); vaccines RTS,S and R21 offer partial protection, and artemisinin resistance is spreading in parts of Africa and Asia. Brazil aims for elimination by 2035.

article.articleHeadline: Oral Fluralaner Clears Screwworm Infestations in Dogs
article.articleSummary: Oral fluralaner (Bravecto) achieved 100% wound clearance in dogs with natural New World screwworm (Cochliomyia hominivorax) infestations in endemic regions of Brazil, according to a multicenter Parasites & Vectors study. Fifteen client-owned dogs received a single oral dose within the approved 25–56 mg/kg range. Twenty-four hours post-treatment, no live larvae remained in any lesions, yielding 100% wound clearance and a total larvicidal efficacy of 94.36% (mortality plus expelled larvae). Of 1,472 larvae collected, 206 were expelled, including 83 alive (5.63%), which were exposed to pupation substrates; none developed into adult flies (0% emergence). No adverse events were reported. The findings suggest an epidemiological benefit beyond individual healing by reducing environmental contamination and supporting integration of isoxazolines into One Health strategies to curb screwworm spread in Neotropical regions.

article.articleHeadline: Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever: Amparo Declares a State of Emergency After Four Suspected Deaths.
article.articleSummary: Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever triggers Public Health Emergency in Amparo, São Paulo, after four suspected 2026 deaths. Four male patients died on July 12; September 29; and October 2 (two on October 2) following treatment in the municipal network. Epidemiological links tied two victims to a pesqueiro in the Chácara São João neighborhood; the site is interdicted and will undergo environmental surveillance, vegetation management, technical mowing, product application, and signage until safety reports confirm reopening. Exposed individuals who visited wooded areas, riverbanks, pesqueiros, pastures, or areas with capybaras should monitor health for up to 14 days; seek care promptly, reporting prior exposure.

article.articleHeadline: Poliomyelitis: Know the Risks and How to Prevent the Disease
article.articleSummary: World Poliomyelitis Day, observed Oct 24, underscores the risks of poliovirus and the critical role of vaccination. Poliomyelitis can cause permanent paralysis and, in severe cases, death. Brazil has not reported wild poliovirus circulation since 1990, but vigilance is needed due to historically suboptimal vaccination coverage. The virus spreads mainly via the fecal-oral route and, when present, may cause fever, malaise, headache, body pains, vomiting, and diarrhea; in some cases, neck stiffness and muscle spasms precede paralysis. The Pan American Health Organization notes about 1 in 200 infections may result in permanent paralysis, often in the lower limbs. Sequelae include weakness, muscle atrophy, growth disturbances, scoliosis, and potential respiratory or speech impairment; rehabilitation can help. Vaccination remains the best prevention; hygiene and sanitation support but do not replace immunization. Brazil uses only inactivated poliovirus vaccine (VIP) since Nov 2024, with a four-dose schedule at 2, 4, 6 months and 15 months; coverage below 95% since 2016.

article.articleHeadline: City Hall intensifies dengue prevention actions in cemeteries for All Souls' Day.
article.articleSummary: Dengue prevention in São Bento do Sul intensifies in municipal cemeteries ahead of All Souls’ Day (Nov 2). article.articleHeadline: Devil's ivy, lucky bamboo, and even Monstera deliciosa: 6 plants that can grow in water and how to care for them so they don't become breeding grounds for the dengue-carrying mosquito
article.articleSummary: As of 26 October 2026, six houseplants—pothos (jiboia), lucky bamboo, peace lily (lírio-da-paz), variegata, Monstera deliciosa (costela-de-adão), and 'swords and spears'—can be grown in water with roots exposed. To prevent dengue transmission by Aedes aegypti, the article emphasizes vigilant maintenance: use stable, transparent vessels, avoid leaves fully submerged, and regularly swap and wash water. For pothos, use a cut with at least one node and keep the node in contact with water while leaves remain above. Lucky bamboo and peace lily require interior cleaning; wash the vessel, monitor root health, and ensure adequate light. Variegata’s leaf patterns should not be submerged; monitor vigor. Monstera deliciosa can propagate from a node cut with a leaf outside. During water changes, discard old water and scrub vessel walls with soap and brush at least weekly to remove mosquito eggs; keep indoor pots clean. The Espírito Santo State Health Department recommends weekly water changes and cleaning.

article.articleHeadline: Prototype kit developed for molecular detection of malaria in remote areas.
article.articleSummary: Peru's National Health Institute leads a project titled 'Optimization of the platform for lyophilized LAMP diagnostic devices: development of a malaria detection kit in Peru', funded with S/ 500,000 by ProCiencia-Concytec. Led by Dr. Pilar Suguimoto Watanabe (Instituto Nacional de Salud) in collaboration with UNTRM’s Amazonas Tropical Diseases Institute and the Amazonas Regional Health Directorate. The aim is a portable malaria diagnostic using lyophilized reagents (LAMP) to reach remote Amazonia with limited lab access. Validation showed analytic specificity 100%, diagnostic sensitivity 98%, and diagnostic specificity 94%, correctly identifying 98% of positives and 94% of negatives, with no cross-reactions observed. Malaria remains a major public health problem in the Peruvian Amazon, with Loreto accounting for most cases: 2025 >33,000; by week 40 of 2026, 18,171. Q1 2026 saw higher P. falciparum shares in Andoas, Pastaza (Datem del Marañón), Trompeteros, and Yaquerana. Next steps include clinical validation, stability studies, scale-up, and regulatory clearance; results were presented Oct 6 at a virtual closing event.

article.articleHeadline: The test came back negative, but he had visceral leishmaniasis, which can be confused with other diseases.
article.articleSummary: Visceral leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania infantum in an 86-year-old man from Rio Grande do Norte, Brazil, died after a negative rapid test and an initial suspicion of a hematologic disease. The patient presented with persistent fever, weight loss, anorexia, fatigue, and pancytopenia with hepatosplenomegaly, prompting consideration of marrow disorders. Diagnosis confirmed only by bone marrow examination revealing the parasite and subsequent PCR. Transmission via sandfly bite; infection targets liver, spleen, and bone marrow, causing anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia. The case, reported by USP and UFRN researchers in Discover Medicine, underscores that a negative rapid test does not exclude visceral leishmaniasis and that rapid diagnosis is crucial to prevent death. The patient died five days after treatment began, highlighting the need for thorough evaluation when clinically suspected despite negative initial tests.

article.articleHeadline: Amazonian Lancehead Snakes Reveal Tongue Worm Parasites Lurking Beyond the
article.articleSummary: Raillietiella furcocerca, a tongue-worm pentastomid, was detected in Bothrops atrox from Tapajós National Forest and surrounding Santarém/Belterra in Pará, Brazil. Recovered from lungs and the coelomic cavity with localized hemorrhages and tissue reactions, the parasite marks the first quantitative baseline for R. furcocerca in B. atrox from the Amazon biome and supports the coelomic cavity as a bona fide infection site, not an artifact of death. Across 48 snakes (28 females, 20 males) examined, 9 were infected (18.8%, 95% CI 9.0–32.6%), yielding 23 parasite specimens, mean abundance 0.48, mean intensity 2.56. Two sampling periods: 2009–2011 (Tapajós) with 37 snakes and 2023–2024 (Santarém/Belterra) with 11 snakes. Infection rose from 8.1% to 54.5%, intensity from 1.00 to 3.33 per infected host. Morphology confirmed by light and scanning electron microscopy.

article.articleHeadline: Tips to Prevent TB Transmission at Home.
article.articleSummary: Tuberculosis (TB) patients managed as outpatients at home should wear a mask to reduce transmission, especially during the first two weeks of treatment when infectiousness is highest. Patients do not need to isolate entirely in a room; they can remain active provided they adhere to therapy and infection-control measures. Close monitoring of household contacts is essential to detect active TB or latent TB infection; those with latent TB can receive preventive therapy to prevent progression, while active TB cases require medical management. Experts recommend patients with confirmed TB to wear a mask around the home for 24 hours if feasible. Cough etiquette and proper sputum disposal are crucial to prevent environmental spread. Prioritize contact tracing for vulnerable groups (children and those with comorbidities). Family support and adherence monitoring are key to recovery; seek healthcare promptly if there is known contact with a TB patient.

Household contact preventive therapy coverage was 19.7%, far from the 80% target. The five-year PHOTON study will enroll over 40,000 participants in Jakarta, Bogor, Depok, and Lombok, plus Tanzania, to evaluate nutritional supplementation as an adjunct to medical TB care and inform future treatment strategies in Indonesia and globally.

article.articleHeadline: Often mistaken for the common flu, recognize the symptoms and dangers of influenza according to the Ministry of Health.
article.articleSummary: As of 26 October 2026, influenza is an acute respiratory infection caused by the influenza virus, distinct from the common cold. In Indonesia (Bandung and Batu), transmission occurs via respiratory droplets from coughing, sneezing, or talking. Common symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose, sore throat, muscle aches, headache, and fatigue; most patients recover within about a week without specific treatment. High-risk groups—children, the elderly, pregnant women, and those with comorbidities—have a higher pneumonia risk. For mild cases, home care involves rest, adequate fluids, balanced nutrition, and regular monitoring; over-the-counter symptom relievers do not kill the virus. Antibiotics are ineffective against influenza. Antivirals such as oseltamivir are reserved for severe disease or high-risk patients per clinician assessment to avoid resistance. Seek hospital care for red-flag signs: high fever lasting >3 days, shortness of breath, chest pain, severe weakness, seizures, dehydration, or deterioration after improvement. Prevention emphasizes handwashing, cough etiquette, masking when sick, and limiting close contact.

article.articleHeadline: Findings of E. coli resistance genes in Banten and the importance of One Health
article.articleSummary: E. coli resistance genes were detected in isolates from the pig slaughtering ecosystem in Banten, Indonesia, signaling a public health alarm for antimicrobial resistance (AMR) across humans, animals, and the environment. In a 2023–ongoing study using whole-genome sequencing, researchers found multidrug resistance (MDR) in E. coli, with about 85% of resistance genes located on plasmids capable of horizontal transfer via conjugation. The findings underscore the food chain as a major route for disseminating resistance. Policy impact is positive: the colistin-resistance gene mcr-1.1, detected in 2023, was not found in 2026, consistent with the policy to stop using colistin in animals. Disturbing precedent aside, the speaker urged prudent antibiotic use for viral illnesses and promoted One Health: integrating human, animal, and environmental health, guided by genomics to map resistance and shape policy.

article.articleHeadline: Foundation models bolster frontline tuberculosis screening.
article.articleSummary: TB screening with chest X-ray AI tools moves from research to clinics. Google AI and Nexus AI deployed a chest X-ray screening tool across six countries in about 40 facilities, processing over 25,000 X-rays with more than 90 clinicians and cutting turnaround to under 45 seconds to speed triage while clinicians retain final diagnoses. The effort covers South Africa, Sierra Leone, and Côte d’Ivoire, with expansion planned in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Zambia, and Cameroon; including on-site screening at the Mponeng gold mine in South Africa. MedGemma, open-weight multimodal models (4B and 27B parameters), together with MedSigLIP, are open-source via the HAI-DEF program, enabling local, offline deployment with downloads over 10 million. Indonesia’s Health Ministry aims to screen 50 million people annually using locally fine-tuned MedGemma/MedSigLIP to keep data in-country. HeAR cough-based acoustic triage is piloting in Zambia (CIDRZ), Ghana (Aurum Institute), and HELINA, complementing imaging in underserved areas.

Improperly cooked chicken can allow Salmonella to enter the body, causing diarrhea, fever, and stomach pain. The World Health Organization defines salmonellosis as a foodborne illness with fever, abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, and sometimes vomiting. While most cases are mild, dehydration can make it life-threatening in children and the elderly. Emphasis on hygiene and proper handling aligns with WHO guidance.

article.articleHeadline: Leptospirosis bacteria endemic in Manila estero | Claudeth Mocon-Ciriaco
article.articleSummary: Leptospira, the agent of leptospirosis, is persistently present along Estero de Paco in Metro Manila, inhabiting both soil and water year-round, not only after floods. A UP Diliman College of Science and Philippine Genome Center study screened 448 bacterial isolates from five sites, finding Leptospira at every location with no significant upstream/downstream or water/soil differences. The researchers identified lipL32-carrying strains, including Leptospira yasudae, a pathogenic lineage, marking the first sequencing of L. yasudae in the Philippines. The complete draft genome (~4.5 million base pairs) was deposited in Microbiology Resource Announcements. Philippine strains appear genetically distinct from the only two other published genomes (Mayotte, Brazil), suggesting a locally evolved lineage. Implications: public health surveillance and interventions must span the entire waterway, as urban leptospirosis risk is year-round; human infection rates were not measured here. article.articleHeadline: EXPLAINER: What is Human Immunodeficiency Virus or HIV?
article.articleSummary: HIV in the Philippines is described as an epidemic by the AIDS Society of the Philippines (ASP) due to accelerating new infections. As of March 2026, the estimated number of people living with HIV (PLHIV) is 288,000. By 2030, the ASP projects that young people aged 15–24 could form the majority of HIV cases if interventions are not implemented. Transmission occurs through infected body fluids; 13 mother-to-child transmission cases were recorded from January to March 2026 (nine male, four female). The ASP emphasizes universal HIV testing for pregnant women to eliminate mother-to-child transmission, with free testing options: Rapid Testing, Self-Testing, Community-Based Screening, and the Rapid HIV Diagnostic Algorithm (rHIVda). ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY (ART) lowers viral load, aligning with U=U — Undetectable equals Untransmittable — and treatment is free under PhilHealth OHAT. Prevention includes PrEP (oral now; injectable soon) and PEP (within 72 hours).

article.articleHeadline: La Libertad reports 6 fatalities and more than 14,000 dengue infections.
article.articleSummary: Dengue in La Libertad, Peru, registers 6 fatalities and over 14,000 infections for 2026, with 665.78 confirmed cases per 100,000 residents and a 0.04% case fatality rate (below 2024’s 0.7% and 2023’s 0.11%). Fatalities stem from Alto Trujillo and Trujillo in Trujillo province, Chao and Guadalupito in Virú, Ciudad de Dios settlement in Guadalupe district, and Pacasmayo province. Trujillo province leads with 8,561 cases in 2026, up 5,088% vs 2025; districts most affected are El Porvenir (1,886), La Esperanza (1,823), Trujillo (1,521), Florencia de Mora (1,421), Alto Trujillo (1,049), Huanchaco (339), Laredo (304), Moche (95), Víctor Larco Herrera (56), Salaverry (52), Simbal (8), and Poroto (3). Virú reports 3,292 cases and 2 deaths (Chao 2,658; Guadalupito 2,010; Virú 425). Pacasmayo totals 764 cases with 2 deaths (San José 308; Guadalupe 306; Pacasmayo 116; San Pedro 28; Jequetepeque 6). Other provinces show smaller totals (Chepén 1,495; Ascope 298; Gran Chimú 34; Pataz 4; Bolívar 2; Santiago de Chuco 1). Since 2021, a positive trend with 2022 and 2025 lacking dengue deaths; drivers include Cyclone Yaku (2023) and 2024 rains. Health authorities urge entry of brigades to destroy Aedes aegypti nests.

article.articleHeadline: The chief epidemiologist of Bashkortostan assessed the risks of monkeypox importation.
article.articleSummary: Azat Mukhametzyanov, Bashkir Ministry of Health’s chief epidemiologist and head physician at Republican Clinical Infectious Diseases Hospital, assessed mpox importation risks into Russia and Bashkortostan. Globally, mpox cases exceed 193,000 since 2022, with Africa as the epicenter; 2026 sees growth in Thailand (over 1,000 since June) and continued activity in Europe and the United States. Transmission is mainly through close physical contact; outside Africa, most patients are adults. In Russia and Bashkortostan the situation is fully controlled. Since 2022, Russia has a robust defense: the Sanitary Shield project conducts sanitary-quarantine control at airports and border checkpoints, and the Perimeter system tracks arrivals from affected countries in real time. Russia also uses domestic diagnostic tests capable of quickly detecting the virus, including new strains. Travelers should avoid contact with wild animals, especially rodents and primates, and maintain hygiene. On return, fever, rash, or lymphadenopathy warrant medical attention, masking, and travel disclosure.

article.articleHeadline: Kenya records second Ebola death as outbreak reaches nine cases
article.articleSummary: Kenya reports nine confirmed Ebola cases and its second death. The latest victim, a 65-year-old woman and close relative of the first patient, died on Friday while receiving treatment; she developed symptoms on October 13 while in quarantine. The first patient, a Kenyan man who had lived in the DR Congo, traveled to Nairobi via Uganda on October 3 and died on October 5 after treatment at several hospitals in the DRC and was later given a safe burial. Seven other patients are receiving treatment at two isolation facilities; all eight secondary cases are linked to the imported case, with no evidence of wider community transmission. Kenya has strengthened border screening and health declaration forms for travelers from DR Congo, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic, while continuing quarantine, isolation, contact tracing, and enhanced screening. As of 26 Oct 2026.

article.articleHeadline: LUMEZI RECORDS ANTHRAX CASES - Zambia 24
article.articleSummary: Three wildlife-confirmed anthrax cases were recorded in Lumezi District, Eastern Province, Zambia—one hippo and two elephants. In response, the government is delivering 12,000 vaccine doses to protect domestic animals, with 11,000 cattle and 1,000 goats slated for vaccination. The exercise is part of a 58,000-dose Eastern Province allocation for five high-risk districts and is planned for the first week of November 2026, targeting more than 1,000 households, with five days of community sensitisation starting next week. Residents are cautioned not to touch wild carcasses or consume game meat from unknown sources; meat should be sourced only from licensed hunting outfits. This comes after last month’s Mpika District outbreak, where 12 people were infected after consuming wildlife meat that tested positive for anthrax. The Lumezi cases are lab-confirmed in wildlife; no human cases have been reported in Lumezi.

article.articleHeadline: Ghana: First Participants Vaccinated With Oxford's Cepi-Backed Lassa Shot in Ghana
article.articleSummary: First participants vaccinated yesterday (25 Oct 2026) at Ghana's Kintampo Health Research Centre in a CEPI-supported trial of Oxford's ChAdOx1 LassaJ vaccine against Lassa fever. The study aims to enroll up to 51 healthy adults aged 18–55 to assess safety and immune response; a parallel trial is underway in Oxford, UK. Lassa fever is a hemorrhagic disease identified in 1969 in Lassa, Nigeria, transmitted mainly via contact with food or items contaminated by Mastomys rat urine/droppings; no licensed vaccine exists. Ghana currently has no outbreak, but cross-border travel with Nigeria keeps regional risk. CEPI funding reaches up to $24.9 million for Oxford's Lassa work; modelling suggests a vaccine across West Africa could save about 3,300 lives over 10 years and avert up to $128 million in societal costs. The Lassa fever Coalition, led by WAHO, coordinates regional vaccine development and introduction.

article.articleHeadline: Ghana Declares Type 2 Polio Outbreak Closed but Urges Parents to Maintain Vaccination | Accra Mail
article.articleSummary: Ghana declared its type 2 poliovirus outbreak closed in August 2026 after outbreak response assessments confirmed interruption of transmission, the Ministry of Health and Ghana Health Service announced during World Polio Day 2026. The closure places Ghana among five African countries that reported ending type 2 poliovirus outbreaks in August 2026, but authorities stress that routine immunisation and surveillance must continue. Ghana reports immunisation coverage above 95% through routine vaccination, supplementary campaigns and community mobilisation, though district-level gaps remain, leaving some children vulnerable if doses are missed. The response involved WHO, UNICEF, Gavi, Rotary International and CDC, focusing on vaccine delivery, monitoring and community engagement. Parents are urged to check vaccination records and seek missed doses; active surveillance remains essential to detect and respond to new risks promptly, ensuring sustained protection for every eligible child.

article.articleHeadline: Cerebral Malaria in Ghana: The Deadly Complication Every Family Should Understand
article.articleSummary: Cerebral malaria, a life-threatening severe malaria complication primarily due to Plasmodium falciparum and transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes, remains a major concern in Ghana. In severe cases, brain involvement causes confusion, drowsiness, seizures, loss of consciousness, or coma, requiring urgent hospital care with injectable artesunate followed by oral antimalarials when stable. While Ghana recorded about 5.9 million malaria cases in 2023 (overall, per WHO), there is no national figure for cerebral malaria. A 2022 Demographic and Health Survey found 8.6% of children under five tested positive for malaria, underscoring transmission risk, but not cerebral malaria prevalence. Risk is highest in young children, though all ages can be affected. Early recognition of warning signs—confusion, seizures, unconsciousness—and prompt testing and treatment are essential. Prevention focuses on insecticide-treated nets and reducing delays in care.
